findings.claim: New finding (pre-existing, not introduced today): legacy AJR codes ZAR (DR Congo) and ROM (Romania) silently drop out of every temperature and 2023-income statistic, so 'Across all 163 countries with both' (draft .md:65) and the 173 / 94 / 69 counts are not the full sets
findings.evidence: Confirmed (check1.py, check2.py). build_analysis.py:61 admits ZAR and ROM as ISO3-shaped codes, and :79-80 then maps gdp and tas by shortnam, so both come back NaN even though COD and ROU exist in both sources. With ZAR mapped to COD and ROM to ROU: former-colony flip -0.4877 (n=94) becomes -0.4794 (n=95), so 'minus 0.49' becomes 'minus 0.48'. Pooled goes from +0.035 (163) to +0.043 (165). Colonial heat r is unchanged, with n 97 to 98 and 98 to 99. Indonesia stays 47th, with a slide of 13.8 to 13.7. DR Congo enters at 46.8 to 5.3, a 41.6-point slide, ranked 22nd of 95. I found a wider class the refuter missed. AJR's WBG (West Bank and Gaza, ex2col 0, sjb1500 12.7) also fails to match the World Bank and ERA5 PSE key. One nuance: the 1995 n=91 and 2023 n=94 samples were already not common before this bug (ERI, VEN and ZAR appear only in 1995; AFG, GNB, LBY, MMR, PNG and SOM only in 2023), so ZAR is one of nine differences, not the cause.

findings.claim: sources.json ajr2002_coef: is the stored document the published article, and does 'Log population density -0.38' support 'They publish a regression coefficient of minus 0.38 with an R-squared of 0.34 on those same 91 countries, which is the same relationship stated a different way'?
findings.evidence: Published version: sources/ajr2002.txt lines 1-4 are the JSTOR cover for QJE Vol. 117, No. 4 (Nov. 2002), pp. 1231-1294. I re-downloaded the MIT URL and its sha256 is 0385c46c...842f4e, the same as the stored PDF; the stored txt hash matches 01f6049d.... The value is in Table V, Panel A, column (1) (base sample, ajr2002.txt line 940). The dependent variable is log GDP per capita (PPP) in 1995, per the Table V header. I also ran AJR's own do-file spec (data/ajr_t5/maketable5.do: keep if ex2col==1; reg logpgp95 lpd1500s) on maketable5.dta. It gives slope -0.3767, R2 0.3413, n=91. For a bivariate OLS, R2 = r^2, and (-0.5842)^2 = 0.341, so 'the same relationship stated a different way' holds. 'AJR do not publish a correlation' also holds: every 'correlat' hit in ajr2002.txt (lines 681, 1000, 1012, 1070, 1767-1770, 2166-2172) is qualitative, and none is a numeric r between 1500 prosperity and income.

findings.claim: sources.json dell2012: published version, and the sentence 'in poor countries a one degree warmer year cut growth that year by about 1.3 percentage points, with no effect in rich countries they could tell apart from zero' (plus 'use year to year weather variation within countries')
findings.evidence: Published version: dell2012.txt line 1 reads 'American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics 2012, 4(3): 66-95' with DOI 10.1257/mac.4.3.66. pdfinfo shows Producer 'Atypon Systems, Inc.' and a CreationDate of 2012-06-12, which fits the AEA typeset PDF. I re-downloaded the nd.edu copy and its sha256 (67eb773d...) equals the stored PDF. The quote is at p. 67 (lines 86-87). The paraphrase is faithful: the unit is 1 degree C; the sign is a reduction; the period is 'in that year'; and 'poor' means below-median PPP GDP per capita in the first year (p. 74, Table 2 note). Table 2's poor-country effect is -1.394 / -1.347. The identification is 'year-to-year fluctuations in temperature and precipitation' (p. 67). On rich countries, p. 67 says changes 'do not have a robust, discernable effect' and p. 76 says not significant, 't-statistics are below 1.0 for all specifications except the last'. One nuance: Table 2 col (5) has 0.561* at the 10% level, and Table 4 col 6 (area weighting) reports a significant zero-lag rich-country effect. So 'robust' is the operative word, but the post's phrase is a fair plain-English version of Dell's own summary.

findings.evidence: Crossref for the DOI returns the same title, The Quarterly Journal of Economics, vol 117, issue 4, pp 1231-1294, 2002, and authors D. Acemoglu, S. Johnson, J. A. Robinson. The DOI 302-redirects to academic.oup.com/qje. On p. 1232 (lines 92-105): 'Our main measure ... is urbanization' (the Bairoch/de Vries argument about agricultural productivity and a transportation network), and density is an 'additional proxy ... relatively more extensive data' whose relation to prosperity 'is more complex'. findings.claim: 'This is Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson's finding (Acemoglu et al., 2002).' The sentence follows directly after the density split (-0.49 on 94 vs +0.28 on 69) and the interaction test ('the test the argument actually rests on').
findings.evidence: The refuter's key premise is false. They say AJR's only test on non-colonies uses urbanisation and never density. AJR Table VI (pp. 1254-1255, which I rendered and rotated as t6b-rot-25.png and t6b-rot-26.png) has columns (9) 'All countries never colonized by Europe' and (10) 'Europe'. Panel C of that table adds log population density in 1500 for those samples: 0.34 (0.07) with n = 43, and 0.37 (0.08) with n = 32. Panel D uses density as the instrument: 0.259 and 0.226. Both are positive, against negative values for former colonies. The text on p. 1253 (ajr2002.txt lines 1033-1040) asks 'Is there a similar reversal among the noncolonies?', finds a positive relationship, and ties the reversal to European colonialism. So the split itself (reversal among colonies, positive among the rest) is AJR's finding. The post's 43-country urbanisation comparison even matches their n of 43. The pooled density-by-colony interaction (t = -5.3) is the post's own construction: AJR's only interactions involve U.K. industrialisation (lines 2003-2070). But the sentence attributes 'the finding', not the test statistic. The next sentence says 'I downloaded their replication files and ran it against 2023 income', which marks the computed figures, including the 2023 interaction, as the author's. The attribution is accurate.
findings.fix: Narrow the sentence to: 'The former-colony reversal is Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson's finding (Acemoglu et al., 2002).'

findings.claim: 'it contains the most famous explanation in this literature, in which a fixed tropical disease environment mattered enormously because of how it shaped European settlement' (gate.toml licence: 'the settler-mortality account, described in the same sentence and attributed to AJR')
findings.evidence: The sentence is at draft lines 106-108: 'it contains the most famous explanation in this literature, in which a fixed tropical disease environment mattered enormously because of how it shaped European settlement'. It names no author and has no in-text citation. The gate.toml licence at line 139 says it is 'attributed to AJR', which is false as written. The description itself matches AJR 2002 pp. 1270-1271 (lines 1826-1845), where they summarise their 2001a work: in high-mortality areas Europeans did not settle and were more likely to build extractive institutions, with malaria and yellow fever named. That 2001 paper is not in the reference list. The only later mention of settler mortality (draft line 248, in the method notes) refers to a data series, not this explanation. So the prominence claim ('most famous ... in this literature') is uncited and has no source in the repo, and the licence's justification is false.
findings.fix: In the draft src, replace 'the most famous explanation in this literature, in which' with 'an explanation in which'. This deletes the uncited prominence claim and keeps the logical point. Then delete or rewrite the gate.toml [claims] line 139 entry, removing 'attributed to AJR'. A second option is to keep the wording and append '(Acemoglu et al., 2002)', which uses an existing reference and describes the account at pp. 1270-1271.

findings.claim: gate.toml licence for 'better land tends to produce more people rather than richer ones': 'the Malthusian premise AJR state on p. 1232' (supports 'AJR raise that caution themselves')
findings.evidence: p. 1232 (ajr2002.txt lines 92-104) has no Malthusian argument, only the remark on urbanisation and that density's relationship is 'more complex'. Malthus appears on p. 1243 (lines 644-652): 'Malthus [1798] argued that high productivity increases population ... So caution [...]'. Note 7 (lines 667-675) is also on p. 1243, since it sits before the 1244 header at line 676, and calls the strict total-income reading 'extreme'. AJR report and qualify Malthus rather than state the premise as their own. So the gate.toml line 142 licence has the wrong locator and wording. The post's own sentence 'AJR raise that caution themselves' (draft line 155) is accurate.
findings.fix: In gate.toml line 142, change the licence to: 'the Malthusian caution AJR raise on p. 1243 and in note 7; hedged by tends to'. No prose change is needed.

findings.claim: Reference: Dell, Jones & Olken (2012), Temperature shocks and economic growth: Evidence from the last half century, AEJ: Macroeconomics 4(3), 66-95, doi 10.1257/mac.4.3.66
findings.evidence: Crossref for 10.1257/mac.4.3.66 returns the same title, American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics, vol 4, issue 3, pp 66-95, issued 2012-07, and authors Melissa Dell, Benjamin F Jones, Benjamin A Olken. The DOI 302-redirects to pubs.aeaweb.org (403 to curl, as sources.json notes). The only citing sentence is checked in SR4. The follow-on statement that it is a within-country result rather than a cross-country ranking is consistent with Dell p. 67, which uses within-country fluctuations to 'isolate its effects from time-invariant country characteristics'.

findings.claim: Reference: McEvedy, C., & Jones, R. (1978). Atlas of world population history. Facts on File. Citing sentence: 'how many people a place supported per unit of arable land, from Colin McEvedy and Richard Jones's population atlas (1978)'
findings.evidence: AJR's bibliography (ajr2002.txt lines 2777-2778) reads 'McEvedy, Colin, and Richard Jones, Atlas of World Population History ([...])'. WorldCat OCLC 4150954 and a scanned title page found by web search agree: Facts On File, New York, 1978; a Penguin edition exists in the UK. AJR p. 1243 (lines 634-636) says the measure divides total population by arable land 'also estimated by McEvedy and Jones', which supports the sentence. Note that this is a secondary citation: the post relies on AJR's account rather than reading the atlas, which the attribution as written does not hide.

findings.claim: Reference: World Bank (2026a). GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international $) [Data set]. World Development Indicators. Citing sentence: NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD, constant 2021 international dollars, for 2023
findings.evidence: data/wb_gdp_2023.json header: sourceid '2' (WDI), lastupdated '2026-07-13', which supports the year 2026. Each row carries indicator {'id': 'NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD', 'value': 'GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international $)'} and date '2023'. The cited URL data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD returns HTTP 200.

findings.claim: Reference: World Bank (2026b). Climate Change Knowledge Portal: Mean surface air temperature, ERA5 annual climatology, 1991-2020 [Data set], plus the method-note description 'near-surface air temperature from the ERA5 reanalysis, annual mean over 1991 to 2020, by country'
findings.evidence: build_analysis.py lines 40-41 record the request: era5-x0.25_climatology_tas_climatology_annual_1991-2020_mean_historical_era5_x0.25_mean/all_countries. I re-fetched it today and got 246 country entries, identical to data/cckp_tas.json, so the description matches the series used. The cited landing URL /download-data returns 403 to curl and WebFetch. The World Bank's own data catalogue, found by web search, names that page as the CCKP route for 'pre-computed statistics for spatially aggregated data ... as API or xls', so the URL is the right venue. The bracketed title is descriptive rather than the portal's literal dataset name, which APA allows for untitled data.

findings.claim: The heat sign flip among former colonies, used as the reason the global chart cannot mean what it looks like. Draft lines 48-51 ('plus 0.29 across 97 ... minus 0.25 across 98 ... The sign flipped'), line 55 ('The flip lives inside the colonised world'), the close at lines 163-165, the excerpt, chart 1's figcaption and chart 2's alt text ('The same thermometer points opposite ways five centuries apart').
findings.evidence: Recomputed with build_analysis.load() (scratch round1/logic-adjudicator/adj.py, adj2.py). The base figures match results.json: heat vs 1500 density among colonies is +0.295 (n=97, t=+3.01) and heat vs income is -0.250 (n=98). Fragility check: dropping Canada alone gives +0.169 (n=96, t=+1.67) and -0.186 (n=97, t=-1.84). Leave-one-out minimum t is 1.67 (CAN); the next lowest is USA at 2.56. Dropping rich4 (USA, CAN, AUS, NZL) gives +0.064 (n=93, t=+0.61) and -0.073 (n=94, t=-0.70). Within African plus Asian colonies (AJR africa/asia dummies) the figures are -0.021 (n=61) and +0.005 (n=62). Spearman is +0.161 (n=97, t about 1.59). A direct test of 'identical across groups', the heat x ex2col interaction on 1500 density, gives t=+3.53 on 173 but only t=+1.38 on 169 without the neo-Europes. On urbanisation the never-colonised show the same heat sign pattern as the colonies: +0.256 then and -0.322 now (n=43), against +0.289 and -0.378 for the colonies (n=43). So 'the flip lives inside the colonised world' (line 55) does not hold on the per-person proxy either. AJR run exactly this exclusion for their own result: sources/ajr2002.txt lines 113-118 ('when we exclude the "neo-Europes"'), and Table V col 6 keeps density at -0.32 on n=87 (line 941). The density flip survives that exclusion: -0.388 (n=90, t=-3.95), interaction t=-4.48 on 159. The post therefore rests its thesis (close lines 163-165, the excerpt, the chart 1 figcaption, the chart 2 alt) on its least robust correlation, and never discloses that fragility.
findings.fix: Delete the heat-flip 'because' clauses so the conclusion rests on interaction.t. In the close (lines 163-165), delete ', because among former colonies that same thermometer used to point the other way: hotter went with more crowded'. In the excerpt, delete ', because among former colonies the same thermometer used to point the other way'. In the chart 1 figcaption (make_charts.chart1), delete 'but among former European colonies the same thermometer ran the OTHER way against the best measure of 1500 prosperity we have, population density, so', leaving 'Nothing after it disputes that the relationship is real; this chart cannot be read as heat acting on prosperity in a way that never changed.' In the chart 2 alt text, delete 'The same thermometer points opposite ways five centuries apart.' The body's figures at lines 48-49 can stay as description. Any statement that the heat flip is robust, or any disclosure of its neo-Europe sensitivity, needs a new bound key (e.g. heat vs density without rich4: +0.06, n=93), so that goes back to the drafter.

findings.claim: 'Heat acting directly and identically on human productivity is the clearest casualty: it should have made the tropics poor in 1500 too, and among the colonised world it did the opposite' (lines 93-95).
findings.evidence: 'Clearest casualty' rests on '+0.29 among the colonised world', which loses significance without Canada (t=+1.67) and vanishes without the neo-Europes (+0.064, n=93, t=+0.61; adj.py). The direct test of heat acting identically across groups is the heat x ex2col interaction on 1500 density. It is t=+3.53 with the neo-Europes and t=+1.38 without them (adj2.py), so the 'identically' half is not clearly rejected for heat once AJR's own exclusion is applied. Outside the colonies, heat vs 1500 density runs the way a constant heat effect predicts: -0.177 globally (n=173, t=-2.36, results.json heat_reversal.all) and -0.211 among the never-colonised (n=76). The disqualification of heat as the sole constant cause does follow from the density interaction (t=-5.33; -4.48 without the neo-Europes), with no need for this sentence's heat correlation. The density-is-wealth sub-point is weaker, because the post carries that proxy as an explicit assumption (design doc 3.4, chart 2 figcaption), so I do not rest the ruling on it.
findings.fix: Replace 'is the clearest casualty: it should have made the tropics poor in 1500 too, and among the colonised world it did the opposite' with 'is a casualty' (lines 93-95). The following sentence and interaction.t carry the point.

findings.claim: Meta description: 'Among former European colonies, hotter places were the more densely settled in 1500.'
findings.evidence: The live MDX metaDescription (line 10) states as a categorical fact a correlation of r=+0.295 (r squared 0.087; heat_reversal.former_colonies.vs_density_1500). Its Spearman is +0.161 (t about 1.59), and it falls to +0.064 without the four neo-Europes (adj.py, see LG1). The body calls a stronger correlation, -0.44, 'a tendency and not a law' (draft line 29). The search-facing sentence gives this weaker one no such qualification.
findings.fix: Narrow it to the bound figure: 'Among former European colonies, temperature and 1500 population density correlate at plus 0.29.' Preferably delete the sentence, in line with the LG1 fix (gate.toml [published].metaDescription and the MDX).

findings.claim: Bold filter, lines 89-90: 'No explanation of the ranking between countries can have an effect that was both constant over the period and the same whether or not Europeans arrived.'
findings.evidence: The bold sentence (draft lines 89-90) forbids any explanation of the cross-country ranking from having a constant, colonisation-independent effect. The counterexample holds logically: income = c*heat + e, and density1500 = c*heat + Z with Z's effect faded. The constant heat term then explains part of the ranking in both eras, and Z produces the inversion. AJR themselves leave room for this structure: sources/ajr2002.txt lines 1724-1730 say geography may have mattered in earlier periods ('the tropics were more productive than temperate areas'). The post's own concessions agree with the narrower reading: line 136 ('does not show that temperature is irrelevant to income') and line 168 ('cannot be the whole of it'). The next sentence (lines 92-93, 'it cannot produce a ranking that inverted') is the correct version. Design doc 3.4 asks 'The filter must be stated precisely'.
findings.fix: Narrow to: 'No explanation of the ranking between countries can rest only on an effect that was both constant over the period and the same whether or not Europeans arrived.'

findings.claim: Close, lines 165-166: 'Whatever explains today's map has to explain that inversion too, and an explanation whose effect never changed and never depended on whether Europeans arrived cannot.'
findings.evidence: 'Whatever explains today's map has to explain that inversion too' (lines 165-166) does not follow. A factor can explain part of today's cross-section while a separate, faded factor accounts for 1500's different ranking: the LG4 counterexample, and AJR's own allowance at sources/ajr2002.txt lines 1724-1730. The claims register's licence for this line ('an effect constant over time and identical across the colonial split cannot invert the ranking within one group (interaction.t)') covers only the second clause. The interaction backs that clause: t=-5.33 on 163 (results.json interaction).
findings.fix: Delete 'Whatever explains today's map has to explain that inversion too, and', leaving: 'An explanation whose effect never changed and never depended on whether Europeans arrived cannot explain that inversion.'

findings.claim: Line 96: 'Outside that world heat did not reverse: across the 69 places measurable in both eras it runs minus 0.15 then and minus 0.04 now, neither clear of chance.'
findings.evidence: On the common 69 the figures are -0.153 (t=-1.27) and -0.041 (t=-0.34) (results.json never_colonised_common_sample, reproduced in adj.py). Two estimates indistinguishable from zero cannot establish that heat 'did not reverse'. On urbanisation, the post's own per-person check (lines 157-158), the never-colonised show the reversal pattern this sentence denies. Heat vs sjb1500 is +0.256 (n=43, t=+1.70) and heat vs income is -0.322 (n=43, t=-2.18), the same signs as the colonies on their common 43 (+0.289, -0.378). On that proxy the contrast 'inverted in one group and not in the other' does not appear for heat.
findings.fix: Delete 'heat did not reverse:', leaving: 'Outside that world, across the 69 places measurable in both eras, heat runs minus 0.15 then and minus 0.04 now, neither clear of chance.'

findings.claim: Chart 1 figcaption: 'against the best measure of 1500 prosperity we have, population density'.
findings.evidence: sources/ajr2002.txt lines 94-100 (p.1232) say urbanisation is AJR's main 1500 measure and density 'an additional proxy'. The draft agrees at line 155: density is 'the wider-coverage second of AJR's two proxies rather than their first'. At line 158 it calls urbanisation 'closer to a per-person measure'. Design doc 3.4 says 'Density is not wealth'. The gate.toml [claims] licence cites p.1232 for 'density as the best 1500 measure', and that page says the opposite.
findings.fix: Delete 'the best measure of 1500 prosperity we have,', leaving 'against population density in 1500' (make_charts.chart1 footnote and the MDX figcaption). If the LG1 fix is applied, this clause goes entirely.

findings.claim: Chart 3 figcaption: 'Their paper used 1995 income and found -0.58 among former colonies'.
findings.evidence: AJR Table V Panel A col 1 prints a coefficient of -0.38 and R2 0.34 on n=91 (sources/ajr2002.txt lines 940-941, 965-966), not a correlation. Draft line 77: 'AJR do not publish a correlation.' The -0.58 is the post's recomputation from their file: results.json flip.density_1500|income_1995|former_colonies.r = -0.5842, n=91. It equals sqrt(0.34), so the relationship is the same, but the chart 3 figcaption ('Their paper ... found -0.58') attributes to the paper a number it does not print, and contradicts the body.
findings.fix: In make_charts.chart3 and the MDX figcaption, change it to 'Their paper used 1995 income; on it, their data give -0.58 among former colonies'.

findings.claim: Chart 3 alt text: 'slopes downward at minus 0.49 across 94 countries ... slopes upward at plus 0.28 across 69'.
findings.evidence: The chart 3 alt text (MDX line 81, gate.toml [published] alt:rf-3) says 'slopes downward at minus 0.49' and 'slopes upward at plus 0.28', which are the correlations (flip.*.r). The slopes are -0.3348 and +0.1477 (results.json flip.*.slope and interaction.slope_former_colonies / slope_never_colonised), and body lines 72-73 report them as minus 0.33 and plus 0.15. The chart 2 alt uses the correct form ('sloping upward, correlation plus 0.29').
findings.fix: Change to 'slopes downward, correlation minus 0.49, across 94 countries' and 'slopes upward, correlation plus 0.28, across 69' (gate.toml [published] alt template and the MDX).

findings.claim: Chart 3 title and draft alt text: 'Being prosperous in 1500 predicts poverty now, but only on one side of the split'.
findings.evidence: The x variable in make_charts.chart3 is lpd1500s, log population density (axis label 'Log population density in 1500'). Design doc 3.4 (docs/2026-09-07-reversal-design.md line 88): 'Density is not wealth ... the post carries it as an assumption.' Draft lines 152-155 say density and income per head 'are not the same quantity'. The suptitle (make_charts.py line 199) and the draft's image alt (line 60) assert prosperity without the assumption, while the body says 'being densely settled in 1500 correlates' (line 70). 'Predicts' in the correlational sense is fine (r=-0.488, t=-5.36).
findings.fix: Change it to 'Being densely settled in 1500 predicts poverty now, but only on one side of the split' (make_charts.chart3 suptitle and the draft alt text). The gate.toml [claims] key changes to match.

findings.claim: Section heading, chart 1 title and draft alt text: 'The tidy story, and it is true'.
findings.evidence: Draft line 5 defines the tidy story as 'the wealth of nations explained by a thermometer', and gate.toml [claims] licenses that phrase as 'describes the reading the post disputes'. The heading at line 13, the alt at line 15 and the PNG title (make_charts.py line 110; I viewed the rendered rf-1 PNG) all read 'The tidy story, and it is true'. The PNG travels standalone above a temperature/income scatter. The body narrows 'true' to the correlation at lines 18-19, the heading does not, and line 168 says 'The thermometer cannot be the whole of it'. This is minor and rhetorical, but it is an internal contradiction.
findings.fix: Narrow it to the correlation: 'The tidy story, and its correlation is real' (draft heading and alt, make_charts.chart1 set_title).

findings.claim: Line 149: 'That minus 0.74 is the measurement of it.' Here 'it' is the split sitting downstream of one side of the comparison and upstream of the other.
findings.evidence: 'It' (lines 147-149) is colonisation sitting downstream of 1500 conditions and upstream of today's income. The -0.74 is lat_abst vs ex2col (results.json colonisation_vs_latitude, r=-0.7416, n=167), so it measures only selection on latitude. The 'downstream of what was already there' leg, 1500 density vs ex2col, is r=-0.350 (n=177, t=-4.94; adj.py). Nothing measures colonisation sitting upstream of income. 'The measurement of it' overclaims.
findings.fix: Narrow it to 'That minus 0.74 measures the latitude part of it.', or delete the sentence.

findings.claim: Lines 99-100: 'Climate sees it extremely well. In this data, absolute latitude correlates with whether a place was colonised at minus 0.74'.
findings.evidence: The post's climate variable, ERA5 temperature, correlates with ex2col at +0.415 (n=203, t=+6.47; adj.py). Only absolute latitude reaches -0.74 (colonisation_vs_latitude). The post itself separates the two at line 194 ('"The equator has not moved" defends latitude; it does not defend the temperature series'). 'Climate sees it extremely well' lends latitude's figure to climate.
findings.fix: Change 'Climate sees it extremely well.' to 'Latitude sees it extremely well.' (line 99).

findings.claim: Lines 148-149: 'partly on things like latitude that shape income today'.
findings.evidence: 'things like latitude that shape income today' (line 148) is causal. The only support is a correlation: lat_abst vs lgdp2023 r=+0.600 on 159 (rivals_common_sample.lat_abst; adj.py reproduces it). The post frames latitude as one of the crude variables that are not an explanation (lines 21-24), and it disclaims causal readings throughout (lines 143-150). The selection argument works with association alone.
findings.fix: Change 'that shape income today' to 'that correlate with income today'.

findings.claim: Chart 1 alt text: 'Singapore, Qatar and Indonesia sit above the line at high temperatures'.
findings.evidence: I refit chart 1's line on all 196 entities (adj.py: slope -0.0602, intercept 10.826, matching tidy_story.slope). Residuals: Singapore +2.58 log points ($130,297 against $9,890 fitted, 100th percentile), Qatar +2.49 ($116,159 against $9,638, 99.5th), Indonesia +0.23 ($13,890 against $11,075, 55th percentile; residual SD 1.05). In the rendered rf-1 PNG, Indonesia's marker sits on the dashed line. Grouping it with two extreme outliers misleads a screen-reader user.
findings.fix: Delete 'and Indonesia', leaving 'Singapore and Qatar sit above the line at high temperatures' (gate.toml [published] alt:rf-1 and the MDX).

findings.claim: Excerpt: 'A chart of temperature against national income is one of the tidiest things in economics, and it is real.'
findings.evidence: The excerpt (MDX line 4, gate.toml [published].excerpt) states 'is one of the tidiest things in economics' with no undercut on tidiness. Its next sentence undercuts the meaning, not the fit. The post's own bound figures contradict the claim: r squared 0.189 (tidy_story.r2_share); incomes within 24-28 C run from $1,133 to $130,297 (spread_24_28c); on a common 159, temperature (-0.46) is beaten by latitude (+0.60) and an Africa dummy (-0.68) (rivals_common_sample). The body treats it as a first impression and undercuts it by line 21. Minor, since it is licensed as rhetorical.
findings.fix: Change 'is one of the tidiest things in economics' to 'looks like one of the tidiest things in economics' in the excerpt.

findings.claim: Excerpt: 'It is also impossible to read the way it invites you to'.
findings.evidence: Body lines 10-11 read 'It is also, I think, impossible to read the way it invites you to'. gate.toml [claims] licenses the thesis as 'hedged "I think"'. The excerpt drops the hedge, and its separate register entry licenses it only by the heat reversal (+0.29 then, -0.25 now), which is not robust to dropping Canada or the neo-Europes (LG1).
findings.fix: Restore the hedge in the excerpt: 'It is also, I think, impossible to read the way it invites you to'. Combine this with the LG1 deletion of the 'because' clause.

findings.claim: Meta description: 'Temperature correlates with national income at minus 0.44.'
findings.evidence: The -0.44 is temperature vs LOG GDP per capita on 196 (tidy_story.r = -0.435). On per-capita dollars it is -0.390 (tidy_story_raw_dollars). The method notes (draft line 180) call the income log 'load-bearing' and say that 'Both matter enormously'. 'National income' also usually means an aggregate rather than income per head. Minor imprecision in the search-facing field.
findings.fix: Change it to 'Temperature correlates with log income per head at minus 0.44.' (gate.toml [published].metaDescription template and the MDX).

findings.claim: Chart 4 figcaption: 'This chart was chosen after the correlations were computed, unlike the first and third'.
findings.evidence: The chart 4 figcaption (MDX line 151) says chart 4 was chosen after the correlations, 'unlike the first and third, and the method notes say so'. The method notes (draft lines 233-235) say the reverse for chart three: 'the same relationship on 1995 income was already sitting in my provenance notes, so it is not a clean case'. docs/provenance-audit.md line 1 says it ran 'before any design', and its table (lines 34-39) already holds density vs 1995 income among colonies at -0.58 (n=91).
findings.fix: Delete 'and third', leaving 'unlike the first, and the method notes say so' (make_charts.chart4 footnote and the MDX).

findings.claim: Method notes, line 233: 'Chart one was specified before its correlation was computed.'
findings.evidence: docs/provenance-audit.md line 1 ('run before any design') and line 55 record an exploratory 'corr(temp1, log GDP 1995) = -0.33'. That is a temperature-against-income correlation already in hand before chart one was specified. It is the same kind of prior exposure that makes chart three 'not a clean case' at draft lines 234-235, and the selection note (line 233) applies a looser standard to chart one. The draft discloses the temp1 run at lines 210-211 but does not connect it. Minor.
findings.fix: Narrow it to 'Chart one was specified before its ERA5 correlation was computed.'

findings.claim: '163 countries' (line 73 and chart 3 alt text), '97 countries' and '94 countries' (line 48 and chart 2/3 alt texts).
findings.evidence: Listing the samples from build_analysis.load() (adj.py, adj2.py): the 94 colonies and the 97/98 heat samples include HKG; the 69 never-colonised include ABW, BMU, CYM and PRI. The 163 therefore contains 5 territories. The draft says '163 countries' (lines 65, 73), and the chart 3 alt and the chart 2 alt ('97 countries') say the same. The post applies the distinction elsewhere: chart 1 says 'countries and territories', and build_analysis.py's hot_and_rich comment records that an earlier draft was corrected for calling territories 'countries'. Minor.
findings.fix: Change '163 countries' and '97 countries' to '163 places' and '97 places' (draft lines 65 and 73, and the gate.toml [published] alt templates for rf-2 and rf-3), or append 'countries and territories'.

findings.claim: Line 70: 'minus 0.49, which is firmly established', and line 73: 'a gap with a t statistic of minus 5.3 ... the test the argument actually rests on'.
findings.evidence: r=-0.488 (n=94, t=-5.36) and interaction t=-5.33 (n=163) reproduce. It survives the hostile checks. Cluster-robust standard errors by tied density value (99 clusters, because the density values come in shared blocks) give t=-4.07, and HC1 gives -5.82 (scratch c2.py). Without the neo-Europes the former-colony figure is -0.39 (t=-3.95) and the interaction t is -4.48 (c4.py). On the common 88, 1995 to 2023 runs -0.588 to -0.498.

findings.claim: Line 70: 'plus 0.28, which is weaker and only just clear of chance'.
findings.evidence: flip.density_1500|income_2023|never_colonised: r=+0.280, n=69, t=+2.39 (two-sided p about 0.02). 'Only just clear' is accurate.

findings.claim: Line 76: '-0.58 across 91 ... -0.49 across 94. It has weakened and it is still there.'
findings.evidence: The samples differ (91 against 94), so a composition effect was possible. On the common 88 former colonies with both incomes: 1995 r=-0.588 (t=-6.74) and 2023 r=-0.498 (t=-5.33) (scratch c2.py). The weakening is real, not a sample artefact. The 2023 sample adds AFG, GNB, LBY, MMR, PNG and SOM.

findings.claim: Line 77: 'AJR do not publish a correlation. They publish a regression coefficient of minus 0.38 with an R-squared of 0.34 on those same 91 countries'.
findings.evidence: ajr2002.txt Table V Panel A column 1: 'Log population density -0.38', R2 0.34, 'Number of observations 91' (lines 940, 965, 966). A text search finds no numeric correlation coefficient in the paper (line 1767 uses the word only in prose). sqrt(0.34)=0.583 against the recomputed 0.584.

findings.claim: Line 21: '-0.44 accounts for about a fifth of the variation in log income, which leaves four fifths somewhere else.'
findings.evidence: r squared = 0.189 (tidy_story.r2_share). It is stated as variance explained, not as a causal share.

findings.claim: Line 21: 'Between 24 and 28 degrees the countries in this chart run from about 1,100 dollars a head to about 130,000.'
findings.evidence: spread_24_28c: n=77, minimum $1,133 (Central African Republic), maximum $130,297 (Singapore).

findings.claim: Lines 21-24: 'temperature is not even the strongest crude variable available ... a continent label beats the thermometer'.
findings.evidence: On the common 159 (rivals_common_sample): temperature -0.464, absolute latitude +0.600, Africa dummy -0.682. All three are on one sample.

findings.claim: Line 27: 'seventeen places above twenty degrees with incomes over forty thousand dollars, ten of them sovereign states and the rest territories'.
findings.evidence: hot_and_rich: 17 entities, 7 of them territories (ABW, BMU, CYM, HKG, MAC, PRI, SXM). Israel at 20.33 C and Australia at 22.15 C clear the threshold (scratch c3.py).

findings.claim: Lines 100-102: '-0.74, which is tighter than any relationship elsewhere in this post ... the tropics are where they went'.
findings.evidence: |r|=0.742 (n=167) exceeds every other correlation in the post. The next largest are the Africa dummy (0.68) and the 1995 former-colony figure (0.58). Of former colonies, 79.2 percent have capitals within 23.44 degrees of the equator, against 7.6 percent of the never-colonised, and 94 percent of tropical places in AJR's file were colonised (scratch c2.py).

findings.claim: Lines 107-108: 'the most famous explanation in this literature, in which a fixed tropical disease environment mattered enormously because of how it shaped European settlement'.
